name: Metamorphoses
teaser: Ovid's poem of transformation — Daphne's laurel, Narcissus's pool, and two hundred myths stitched into one river of change. The encyclopedia of classical mythology, told with wit and sorrow.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening books — creation and the first metamorphoses
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening books, where creation gives way to the first transformations. Notice how Ovid treats change as both punishment and poetry. Write what the theme of metamorphosis lets the poem say about desire, power, and the refusal to stay still.

name: Inferno
teaser: The first canticle of Dante's Divine Comedy — the descent through the nine circles of Hell, from the uncommitted to the traitors in ice. The most vivid moral landscape ever imagined.

exploreAction.targetName: Cantos I–V, the entrance and the first circles
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening cantos, where Dante enters the dark wood and passes through the gates of Hell. Notice how each circle's punishment fits its sin. Write what the contrapasso reveals about Dante's sense of justice — and where you would place yourself.

name: The Canterbury Tales
teaser: Chaucer's 14th-century frame of pilgrims telling stories on the road to Canterbury — the Knight, the Wife of Bath, the Pardoner, and the Miller. The book that made English literature possible.

exploreAction.targetName: The General Prologue and the Wife of Bath's Tale
exploreAction.instruction: Read the General Prologue, where the pilgrims are sketched in a few lines each, then the Wife of Bath's prologue and tale. Notice how the teller and the tale play off each other. Write what the frame's variety says about Chaucer's England — and about storytelling itself.

name: Paradise Lost
teaser: Milton's 1667 epic of the fall of man — Satan's rebellion, the war in Heaven, and the expulsion from Eden, written as the poet went blind. The poem that made the devil literature's most magnetic character.

exploreAction.targetName: Book One — the council in Hell
exploreAction.instruction: Read Book One, where Satan rallies the fallen angels in Hell. Notice how Milton's blank verse builds its own music. Write what the poem gains by giving evil the best speeches — and what the epic argues about freedom, obedience, and the uses of grief.

name: A Midsummer Night's Dream
teaser: Shakespeare's comedy of four lovers, a fairy king and queen, and a weaver transformed — the play where the forest's magic untangles the heart's confusions. The most joyful night in the theatre.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the final act
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the lovers' tangles are set, then the final act with the mechanicals' play. Notice how the fairy magic both mocks and mends the humans' chaos. Write what the play suggests about love's unreasonableness — and why it is best played at night.

name: The Tempest
teaser: Shakespeare's late romance of the exiled magician Prospero and the island he rules — the storm he raises, the spirits he commands, and the forgiveness he finally chooses. The play about art, power, and letting go.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One — the storm and the island
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where the storm and the island's inhabitants are established. Notice how Prospero controls the play's magic as a playwright controls a stage. Write what Prospero's renunciation at the end — the drowning of his book — suggests about art and power.

name: Othello
teaser: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Moor and his ensign Iago — the handkerchief, the poison of suspicion, and the murder of innocence. The play about race, trust, and the evil of small insinuations.

exploreAction.targetName: Act One and the jealousy scenes of Act Three
exploreAction.instruction: Read Act One, where Othello's love and Iago's grievance are established, then the scenes where the poison works. Notice how Iago turns Othello's own strengths against him. Write what the play says about the power of suggestion, and about the tragedy of trust betrayed.

name: Sense and Sensibility
teaser: Austen's 1811 first novel of the Dashwood sisters — Elinor's restraint and Marianne's passion, tested by poverty, love, and the weather of feeling. The novel that balances two ways of being alive.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the inheritance and the move
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where the sisters' temperaments and their reduced fortunes are established. Notice how Austen stages the argument between sense and sensibility in every scene. Write what each sister teaches the other — and which one you would rather be.

name: Northanger Abbey
teaser: Austen's 1817 novel of Catherine Morland, whose head is full of Gothic novels and who expects the abbey to be haunted — a satire of reading itself, and the funniest of Austen's books.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the heroine who is not one
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Austen introduces Catherine as an unheroic heroine and her novel-bred expectations. Notice how the narrator jokes about fiction even while writing it. Write what the novel says about the difference between stories and life — and why the distinction matters.

name: Mansfield Park
teaser: Austen's 1814 novel of Fanny Price, the poor cousin raised among the Bertrams — quiet, principled, and finally right. Austen's most serious novel, and the one she called the most difficult to write.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — Fanny's arrival at the Park
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where shy Fanny is transplanted into the great house. Notice how Austen builds the moral contrast between Fanny's constancy and the household's ease. Write why the novel's quiet heroine is so often contested — and what her steadiness is worth.

name: Lady Susan
teaser: Austen's early epistolary novella of the brilliant, amoral widow Lady Susan Vernon, who schemes through letters with total self-possession — Austen's wickedest heroine, and the book she never published.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening letters, where Lady Susan's maneuvering begins. Notice how the letter form lets Austen show her schemes and her allies' misreading simultaneously. Write what the novella reveals about Austen's comic cruelty — and why she may have kept it private.

name: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
teaser: Fielding's 1749 comic epic of the foundling Tom Jones, expelled from Paradise Hall and sent on the road to London — a laughing, sprawling novel about appetite, honor, and the education of a good heart.

exploreAction.targetName: The opening chapters — the foundling and the narrator's promise
exploreAction.instruction: Read the opening chapters, where Fielding introduces his hero and his narrator with a wink. Notice how the narrator's asides turn the novel into a conversation. Write what the novel's claim — that a foundling's heart can outrank a gentleman's birth — meant in 1749.
